catalog_quote: Der dynamische Akzent wird im nachstehenden mit dem Zeichen ´ kennbar gemacht. Sehr wichtig ist es, jedes Wort richtig zu betonen; denn je nach der Tonstellung erhält das Wort manchmal eine ganz andere Bedeutung, z. B.: kará Liebe, kára Mond, dúpui er hat es gewaschen, dupúi es ist entsprossen, puántaansi ich habe ihn fallen getan, púantaansi ich habe „Wind entlassen“, dúmari ich habe mich gebadet, dumári ich bin nach Hause gegangen usw. In manchen zweisilbigen Wörtern stehen beide Silben auf gleicher Tonstufe, wie dua Sonne, karaṅ Krebs, mutu blind, apo Regen, nankai Zauberer, nantoṅ Leute usw. Im allgemeinen wird die Betonung sehr schwach gehalten, in diesen Fällen hat keine der beiden Silben ein Akzentzeichen. Wenn ein drei- oder mehrsilbiges Wort den Akzent auf der zweiten (bzw. dritten) Silbe hat, so ist diese Silbe hochtonig und auch alle vorhergehenden Silben sind hochtonig; die ihr nachfolgenden Silben dagegen sind tieftonig. || p. 964: B. Die Koromira-Mundart. (Nur insofern sie von der Nasioi-Mundart abweicht.) || Hurd & Hurd 2020 [1970] p. 1 (Naasioi Proper): Stress is nonphonemic. With words in isolation it occurs on the first syllable of two-syllable words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Der dynamische Akzent wird im nachstehenden mit dem Zeichen ´ kennbar gemacht. Sehr wichtig ist es, jedes Wort richtig zu betonen; denn je nach der Tonstellung erhält das Wort manchmal eine ganz andere Bedeutung, z. B.: kará Liebe, kára Mond, dúpui er hat es gewaschen, dupúi es ist entsprossen [...]. In manchen zweisilbigen Wörtern stehen beide Silben auf gleicher Tonstufe [...]. Im allgemeinen wird die Betonung sehr schwach gehalten [...]. Wenn ein drei- oder mehrsilbiges Wort den Akzent auf der zweiten (bzw. dritten) Silbe hat, so ist diese Silbe hochtonig und auch alle vorhergehenden Silben sind hochtonig; die ihr nachfolgenden Silben dagegen sind tieftonig.
new_statements.translation: The dynamic accent is marked in what follows with the sign ´. It is very important to stress every word correctly, for depending on the position of the accent a word sometimes gets an entirely different meaning, e.g. kará 'love', kára 'moon', dúpui 'he has washed it', dupúi 'it has sprouted' [...]. In some disyllabic words both syllables stand on the same pitch level [...]. In general the stress is kept very weak [...]. When a word of three or more syllables has the accent on the second (or third) syllable, that syllable is high-toned and all preceding syllables are also high-toned; the syllables following it, on the other hand, are low-toned.
new_statements.citation: Rausch, P. J. 1912. Die Sprachen von Südost-Bougainville, Deutsche Salomonsinseln. Anthropos 7: 105-134, 585-616, 964-994. [Author writing from the Koromira mission station; accent paragraph in section A 'Die Nasioi-Sprache', Lautlehre d) Akzent; section B 'Die Koromira-Mundart' (pp. 964-974) is described 'nur insofern sie von der Nasioi-Mundart abweicht' and lists no difference in accent.]
new_statements.locator: p. 107 (pdf page 131 of the archive.org volume scan anthropos_1912_7), section A, Lautlehre, 'd) Akzent'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened (extracted text) and the page scan. Printed p. 107 carries the header "Die Sprache von Südost-Bougainville, Deutsche Salomonsinseln. 107" and the sub-section "d) Akzent." The reported quote is there verbatim; the bracketed [..] elisions cover only the further minimal pairs (puán-taansi/púantaansi), the list of level disyllables (dua, karaṅ, mutu, apo, nankai, nantoṅ) and the clause "in diesen Fällen hat keine der beiden Silben ein Akzentzeichen". Accents kará/kára, dúpui/dupúi, dúmari/dumári are legible on the image. Section context: this is section A "Die Nasioi-Sprache", Lautlehre; it states that accent position can change word meaning, that some disyllables have both…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Rausch (Nasioi proper, extended to Koromira by his 'only where it differs' framing): accent position is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs kará/kára, dúpui/dupúi, dúmari/dumári), no positional rule is given, the accent is weak, some disyllables have no accent at all, and the accented syllable plus everything before it is high-pitched with following syllables low. Rausch's Koromira forms carry accents on various syllables (káiro, nárun, kéintakára, uó, narúnta). The later SIL description of Naasioi proper (Hurd & Hurd 1970/2020, p. 1) contradicts this: stress nonphonemic, first syllable of disyllables, second syllable of words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Rausch. Rausch marks two accents in kéintakára '2 (persons)' (Koromira, p. 964) without comment. Hurd & Hurd say nothing on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Rausch: some disyllables have both syllables level (dua 'sun', karaṅ 'crab', mutu 'blind', apo 'rain', nankai 'sorcerer', nantoṅ 'people') and get no accent mark; a note in the Nasioi verb section (Anthropos 7, part 2) says the accent shifts when the second perfect takes the syllable -nu. Hurd & Hurd (Naasioi proper): stress is nonphonemic; rule stated for words in isolation only.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (Rausch: 'jedes Wort'; Hurd & Hurd: 'words in isolation'). Neither statement is about Koromira first-hand: Rausch's is for Nasioi with Koromira as a 'Mundart' described only where it deviates (no stress deviation listed); Hurd & Hurd's is explicitly for the Naasioi Proper dialect (Darutue), with Koromira merely named among eight dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Nasioi/Naasioi proper (naas1242), not Koromira first-hand. Rausch 1912 (Glottolog's only descriptive reference for koro1313; author resident at Koromira station) presents Koromira as 'Die Koromira-Mundart', a dialect of Nasioi described 'nur insofern sie von der Nasioi-Mundart abweicht', and its Koromira section (pp. 964-974) has no accent statement, only accent-marked forms; so the Nasioi 'Akzent' paragraph (p. 107) applies to Koromira only by that framing. Hurd & Hurd 1970/2020 likewise list Koromira as one of eight Naasioi dialects but base their (contradictory) stress statement on Naasioi Proper (Darutue village). Whether the catalog should carry a koro1313 entry inherited from naas1242 is a lumping decision for the catalog owner; if it does, the two Nasioi statements disagree (1912 lexically contrastive vs 1970 nonphonemic positional).

sources.note: Nothing. The Koromira Lautlehre (p. 964, verified on the page scan) is a phoneme table plus vowel notes; no sentence on stress/accent anywhere in pp. 964-974 (the only 'Betonung' hit on p. 974 belongs to the Uruava section starting on that page). Koromira forms carry acute accent marks (káiro '4', nárun '1 m.', kéintakára '2 persons', uó '5 persons', narúnta, kéno, aréin, arévai, okénupan, maréki, dakéni) but no rule is stated; by the section's own framing, anything not listed 'lautet wie in der Nasioi-Mundart'.

sources.citation: Hurd, Conrad & Phyllis Hurd. 2020 [1970]. Naasioi verbs, ed. Masayuki Onishi. SIL International Language and Culture Archives (revision of the paper published in Oceanic Linguistics 9, 1970). Sec. 2 'Phonemes', p. 1; note 1, p. 42.
sources.note: p. 1: 'Stress is nonphonemic. With words in isolation it occurs on the first syllable of two-syllable words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables.' Stressed vowel in identical-vowel sequences has higher pitch. Note 1 (p. 42) lists eight dialects of Naasioi including Koromira, but 'This paper is based on the dialect of Naasioi Proper' (Darutue village). Contradicts Rausch on contrastiveness; describes Nasioi proper, not Koromira.
